content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the relationship between differential privacy and adversarial robustness. Focusing on linear classifiers and intercept learning, the paper provides a series of theoretical results showing that at a certain attack radius, the DP classifier can achieve highest adversarial robustness. The empirical studies go beyond linear settings and examine the robustness and privacy of deep nets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The paper studies an interesting problem 
- The paper is well-written

Weaknesses:
- The abstract incorrectly summarizes the main result. "While previous works have postulated that privacy comes at the
cost of worse robustness, we give the first theoretical analysis that DP models can indeed be robust and accurate, even sometimes more robust than their naturally-trained non-private counterparts." However, the theoretical result shows that there exists some attack radius such that the DP classifier is most adversarially robust. In fact, looking at the proof, the theory holds for any classifier such that $b_{DP}<b_0$. The theoretical results do not conflict with previous works as they may not examine the right radius where the DP classifier is the most robust. 

- It is unclear how the privacy budget ($\epsilon$) affects robustness.

- It'll be great if the paper can further clarify the practical usefulness of the theoretical result. Particularly, is the radius where the DP classifier is the most robust practically useful? Is this a small value that a regularly-trained classifier can also be robust while maintaining good accuracy? Is it a large value that even an adversarially trained classifier cannot be robust? Or else?

- There is a gap between theory and experiments: (1) theory studies the linear classifier and intercept learning while the experiments fine-tune all layers of a neural network. (2) theory shows that one can search for a radius that achieves maximal robustness while experiments search for hyperparameters of a DP optimizer for a fixed radius.

- DP learning often experiences a variation of performance in different independent runs due to the stochasticity during learning. It is not clear whether the result in the experiment section is averaged over multiple runs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarify, Quality, and Novelty is good. The reviewer has concerns about reproducibility as detailed above.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. We agree that the regime where DP models are more robust than naturally trained models is limited. Yet it is important to note that previous works all claim that DP worsens robustness. Our key contribution is to contradict this claim by introducing new possibilities.

To address your comment "It is unclear how the privacy budget affects robustness.", we would like to emphasize that this works' focus is *not on the privacy budget but on the private optimization*: the subtle difference is that, even for privacy budget that does not make sense in practice, say $\epsilon=\infty$, we still claim that DP-trained (with the per-sample gradient clipping but zero noise, see Figure 3 blue bars) models can be comparably robust to naturally trained models.

We highlight that the most practically important theorem is Thm 3: we don't require DP models to be the most robust, but just equally or more robust than naturally trained models *at a fixed attack radius*. The range of this phenomenon is wide (see Table 1&3). However, DP-trained models are not expected to beat adversarially trained models (maybe on-par with the latter when the attack is not strong). As we discussed in the final section, DP training and adversarial training are orthogonal, so they can be combined as in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.02265.pdf

To address your comment "There is a gap between theory and experiments: (1) theory studies the linear classifier and intercept learning while the experiments fine-tune all layers of a neural network. (2) theory shows that one can search for a radius that achieves maximal robustness while experiments search for hyperparameters of a DP optimizer for a fixed radius.", we point out that the CIFAR10 experiment is using SIMCLR with only last layer trained. This is clearly presented in Line 4 of Section 4, thus the neural network is exactly a linear model! Therefore, there is no gap between theory and this part of experiments. Also, we again emphasize our Thm3: our goal is to verify at fixed attack radius and show DP model is comparably if not more robust than natural model. To assure the reviewer, Table 1&3 can also be used to support Thm2, where we do "search for a radius that achieves maximal robustness".

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies the adversarial robustness property of private learning models and claims that private models can be more robust than the associated non-private ones when (1) some appropriate parameters are chosen, (2) public data is available, and (3) suitable choices of DP optimizers. 
To understand why private models can be more robust, the paper considers a mixture of two Gaussians and derives robust and standard errors.  The evaluation illustrates the behavior of private and non-private models on different adversarial attacks and a robustness metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
+ Should hold for more general cases, the finding reported is significant. It would illustrate some hidden benefits of private models. 
+ The experiments are extensive, and compare different base models, different attacks, and several privacy budgets. 

**Weaknesses**
- At the beginning of Section 3.2, the paper makes a very strong assumption: only the intercept `b` is learned in private ways. Hence, it disregards the impact of adding noise to the model coefficients. My suggestion would be to resolve this issue by considering only 1D data, where the parameters coincide with the intercept. Although this would also render the theoretical finding much more specific. 

- In Theorem 2, the paper seems to consider a single realization of private b_{DP}. Since this is a random variable, b_{DP} can be greater than b_0.  Additionally, the analysis focuses on this single realization of b_{DP}, instead of considering the distribution over b_{DP}. 
A more appropriate analysis In Theorem 3 should consider the expected robust error, instead of a single robust error obtained by some arbitrary random seed. 

- In Section  3.2, in *DP optimization can lead to robustness *, the paper claimed that the gradient vanishes when the private training reaches a stationary point. However, using gradient clipping, private models might not converge, as shown, for example in [3]. 

- In the experiments, the trends for CelebA (Table 3) appear weak -- in several cases, the non-private models have higher robust accuracy than the private ones. Can the authors explain why this happens?




[3] X Chen, et al. Understanding Gradient Clipping in Private SGD: A Geometric Perspective. In NeurIPS 2020.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is relatively well written

The source code is missing, which may impact reproducibility.

Some important related work was not discussed, for example [1], [2]

[1] H Phan, et al. Scalable differential privacy with certified robustness in adversarial learning. In ICML 2020.
[2] H Phan, et al. Preserving differential privacy in adversarial learning with provable robustness. In 2019.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your comment. We indeed consider a deterministic $b_{DP}$ in Theorem 2, because we followed "On the Convergence and Calibration of Deep Learning with Differential Privacy" where the noise $\sigma$ has small influence on the convergence. This is reflected in our Figure 3: the randomness of $b_{DP}$ is characterized by the bar. 

We agree that DP optimization may not converge, but in our bias-only linear classifier scenario, we observe that this is not the case. Furthermore, our claim *DP optimization can lead to robustness* is also supported by the extensive experiments: maybe in some of them DP optimization does not converge, but the robustness is supported.

There are two possible explanations for the phenomenon in CelebA (Table 3): unlike Table 1 (CIFAR10), where SIMCLR only has its last linear layer optimized, here the model is fully optimized so non-DP model under zero attack should have stronger accuracy than DP, and this "better accuracy regime" may endure a bit when the attack is weak.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on studying the robustness of DP-preserving models against adversarial examples in a setting of binary classifiers. Experimental results were conducted on three benchmark datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The topic is significant. However, the paper has several major weaknesses, as follows:

- The paper claims this is the first theoretical analysis of the connection between DP-preserving models and their robustness against adversarial examples. Indeed, this claim is incorrect. The connection between DP and certified robustness against adversarial examples has been studied since 2019 [1, 2, 3]. This paper does not advance, discuss, or even compare these studies. The observation that DP-preserving models enhance (certified) robustness is well-known.

- There is a big gap between the proposed analysis (binary classifiers given a mixed Gaussian distribution) and the experiments. First, the analysis is too simple compared with deep neural networks and complicated datasets in real-world applications, and section 4 does not address this gap. So, I am wondering whether the analysis in the paper is realistic or not. Extending it to non-linear classifiers such as neural networks is not straightforward, even if applicable. 

- The results on CIFAR-10 appear to be lower than [3] even compared with certified accuracy. That highlights the importance of covering the literature. In addition, there is no clear explanation why the authors achieve Theorems 1-3. What are the key reasons or insights of these Theorems? How could we extend them to cover non-linear classifiers and deep neural networks? In which scenarios Theorems 1-3 do not work? 

- Experimental results must be extended to cover more complicated datasets, such as ImageNet. Also, state-of-the-art baselines, such as state-of-the-art randomized smoothing (e.g., [4]) and [1, 2, 3], are needed.

[1] Mathias Lécuyer et al. "Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy." S&P'19

[2] NhatHai Phan et al. "Heterogeneous Gaussian Mechanism: Preserving Differential Privacy in Deep Learning with Provable Robustness." IJCAI'19.

[3] NhatHai Phan et al. "Scalable Differential Privacy with Certified Robustness in Adversarial Learning." ICML'20.

[4] Horvath et al. "Boosting Randomized Smoothing with Variance Reduced Classifiers." ICLR'22.

content.title: Reviewer has completely misunderstod this work
content.comment:
We are deeply concerned that the reviewer fails to understand DP, judging by the comment "The connection between DP and certified robustness against adversarial examples has been studied since 2019 [1, 2, 3]." Thus, we doubt this review reflects the 5 confidence score.

DP discussed here is the classic **per-example differential privacy** as in "Deep learning with differential privacy" by Abadi et al. and "The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy" by Dwork et al. To be clear, the DP model confuses the attacker whether any single sample is used during the training. Therefore, **none of the reviewer's references is relevant**: [1,2] uses the mathematical tool from DP to study **per-pixel** defense, which is termed specifically as PixelDP in their paper; [3] studies the **per-batch** defense, therefore using the name 'Stochastic Batch Mechanism' in the title, plus the method is unnecessarily complicated and not well-recognized in the DP deep learning literature. We emphasize that the relevant works have been discussed in our submission.

[4] is an orthogonal direction to our work. As we claimed, we compare DP trained models to naturally trained models, both can be adversarially trained or randomly smoothed. We don't want to mix up techniques but randomized smoothing may be interesting for future work.

To address "In addition, there is no clear explanation why the authors achieve Theorems 1-3. What are the key reasons or insights of these Theorems? How could we extend them to cover non-linear classifiers and deep neural networks? In which scenarios Theorems 1-3 do not work?"

We have **explained Theorem 1-3 clearly in bold text**, listing the assumptions and insights. Deep neural networks are sometimes linear in parameters. For example, in the neural tangent kernel regime, deep neural networks evolve like a linear model, known as the linearized network; in Section 4, we explicitly stated "Notably, several state-of-the-art advances are actually achieved by linear classifiers within the deep neural networks (Mehtaetal.,2022; Tramer&Boneh,2020), i.e. by finetuning only the last linear layer of neural networks"; in Section 5, previous SOTA DP accuracy is achieved by SimCLR last-layer finetuning, which is exactly a linear model.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The experiment is solid and the paper is easy to read

Weakness: The definition of adversarial robustness in this paper may not be the standard way of defining it. If so, more justifications should be made. In the standard definition of adversarial attacks, an input $x$ is robust to $l_d$-norm attacks of size $L$ if for any $x'$ such that $||x-x'||_d \leq L$, it always has $f(x) = f(x')$, where $f$ is the predictor. I didn't find a clear mathematical definition of robustness in this paper. From equation (3), I guess the definition in the paper is different, where the requirement $f(x') = f(x)$ is changed to $f(x') = f(x)$ with somewhat probability. If my guess is correct, then, the experimental part makes no sense because the attacks are for the standard robustness definition in stead of the definition proposed in this paper.

PS: All my evaluation assumes that my guess about the robustness definition is true. Please correct me if I am wrong.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for your comment. We assure you that our adversarial robustness notion is standard. To correct your comment "an input  is robust to $l_d$-norm attacks of size L if for any x' such that $||x'-x||_d<L$, it always has $f(x)=f(x')$, where $f$ is the predictor." In fact, following the definition in NeurIPS 2018 tutorial (https://adversarial-ml-tutorial.org/introduction), the definition should be $y(x)=f(x')$, i.e. comparing the predictor to the label $y$.

With this notion in place, we are studying the robust accuracy as the percentage of robust examples, or equivalently the ($1-$robust classification error) in Equation (3). This is where we defined the standard adversarial robustness.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper revisits the question of whether training models with privacy guarantees should hurt robustness.
The paper first considers a simple formal binary classification setting and shows that training with DP can lead to classifiers with optimal robustness.
Then, the paper performs an empirical evaluation of the robustness of models trained with DP-SGD across a range of hyperparameters and shows that some choices lead to models with high robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
(+) The connection between privacy and robustness is interesting and worth studying empirically
(+) The paper claims to achieve significant robustness with DP-SGD
(-) The theory part of the paper has essentially nothing to do with privacy
(-) The empirical results seem very suspicious. Given such extraordinary claims, some more supporting evidence is warranted
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is generally easy to understand. The experimental setups are detailed well enough to allow for reproducibility.
The paper's take is sufficiently novel: it revisits prior empirical works that showed that training with DP hurts robustness, and aims at showing the opposite, both formally and empirically.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While a few papers have looked at the empirical effect of DP-SGD on robustness, existing results seem preliminary and incomplete and so this question definitely merits further study.

The paper starts with a theoretical analysis of a simple binary classification problem, and aims to show that DP does not necessarily hurt robustness in this setting.
But such a statement is only really interesting if we consider a setting with finite training data. In the information-theoretic regime considered here, it doesn't make sense to talk of a "private" classifier. There is no (explicit) training data so any classifier considered is trivially private.
The formal analysis amounts to showing that the Bayes-optimal classifier for perturbations of size \gamma has an intercept equal to b_\gamma (which is a monotone function of \gamma). And so if the DP classifier (which, again, is not well defined since there is no training set here) learns some intercept b_DP, then this classifier will be Bayes-optimal for perturbations of some specific size.
But that same can be said for *any* classifier in this setting. Nothing in the analysis here has any bearing on privacy in any way.
And so the entire theory part of the paper essentially says *nothing* about the tradeoff between models trained with differential privacy and robustness.

The empirical part of the paper shows that the robustness of models trained with DP-SGD depends highly on the choice of hyperparameters.
All experiments start with a pre-trained SimCLR model, which is then finetuned with DP-SGD on CIFAR-10.
The paper claims that with the right choice of learning rate and clipping norm, this procedure leads to significant adversarial robustness. In fact the obtained robustness is not too far off from that obtained with adversarial training (without DP), and way better than for models trained without DP-SGD.

Simply put, I find these results extremely hard to believe given all the prior literature on adversarial robustness.
In the existing literature, adversarial training is virtually the only training approach that confers significant adversarial robustness. That a simple combination of: a good learning rate, gradient clipping and small gradient noise would be enough to get similar results seems far-fetched. This is especially curious here because the original pre-trained model, SimCLR, is not known to be robust to adversarial examples on its own. And yet, Table 1 claims that even without DP, a simple hyperparameter search for finetuning leads to a model with >50% robust accuracy for perturbations of size 4/255. This is very hard to believe.

To be fair, I can't point to any obvious mistake in the paper's evaluation. But there a few curious things:
- In Table 2, the results of all l-inf attacks are suspiciously close. In fact, BIM, PGD and APGD often get the exact same robust accuracy, down to 0.01%. Empirical evaluations with these attacks are always a bit noisy so this seems very strange. Moreover, the iterative attacks essentially perform no better than FGSM (at least not by more than 1%).
- There is no evaluation with any gradient-free attacks. I would recommend running the models through AutoAttack to get more confidence in the robustness evaluations.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments! We agree that the theory part is in the information-theoretic regime, and there are no explicit training data rather than the data distribution. In this regime, we are studying the DP-SGD as an algorithm and the robustness of the parameters found by this algorithm. That is, the privacy itself may not make sense when there is no explicit data, but the robustness of the results from DP-SGD (especially the per-sample gradient clipping) is still analyzable.

We also agree that DP-trained classifiers, with the correct hyperparameters, can oftentimes outperform naturally trained classifiers, sometimes on-par-with adversarially trained classifiers. Notice that DP training and natural training are mutually exclusive, but DP training and adversarial training are not. It would be interesting to combine the DP adversarial training in future work.

We confirm that the experiments results are solid. We identify 2 reasons of the strong robustness from DP classifiers:
1. DP models seem to be robust when the attack is weak or moderate. Under stronger attacks, DP models are less robust than adversarially trained models on moderate attack (e.g. l infinity 8/255 in Table 1).
2. In Table 1&2, the model is the pretrained and **frozen** SIMCLR, where only the last linear layer is trained! Empirically, linear models are more robust than deep neural networks. This may explain the robustness of DP models that surprises you. We refer you to Table 3 where non-frozen fully fine-tuned ResNet and VisionTransformer are vulnerable to l infinity 2/255 attacks.

Your comments are very helpful and we will include them in the next revision.
